planting.note: Plant divisions in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in bright shade to full shade; Empress is noted for producing the largest flowers of any common toad lily cultivar, on an upright clump well suited to a shaded border's mid-height layer.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in bright shade to full shade; Empress bears extra-large, wide-opening, spidery flowers up to an inch and a half across, white with deep purple-red spotting, noticeably larger than most other toad lily cultivars and striking enough to draw close inspection. It flowers in late summer into fall on an upright, thirty-inch clump, providing fresh color in the shade garden as most other perennials are winding down. Keep soil evenly moist and mulch with leaf litter to mimic its native woodland floor conditions, and divide congested clumps in spring if flowering begins to decline. Combine with hostas, ferns, and other fall-interest shade perennials for a layered woodland display.

planting.note: Plant dormant crowns in October–November in zone 9 for a winter-into-spring crop; Ruby June is a patented Lassen Canyon Nursery release bred specifically for the Southeast and Gulf region, with disease resistance and a compact, tidy plant habit.

directions: Plant dormant crowns with the crown at soil level in raised, well-drained beds in full sun; Ruby June is a short-day strawberry bred specifically for the Southeast and Gulf region, combining disease resistance with a compact, tight plant architecture that keeps beds tidy and makes picking easier than more sprawling cultivars. The berries are deep ruby-red both inside and out, with high early-season yield that gets a Gulf South winter strawberry planting off to a strong start. Like other short-day strawberries in zone 9, treat it as a winter annual, planting fresh crowns each fall for harvest through winter into spring. Maintain consistent drip irrigation and raised, well-drained beds to reduce disease pressure typical of humid Gulf Coast strawberry production.
sources: Lassen Canyon Nursery — US Plant Patent PP27190

common_name: Florida127 Strawberry (Sweet Sensation, UF/IFAS Winter Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant dormant crowns in October–November in zone 9 for a winter-into-spring crop; Florida127 (marketed as Sweet Sensation) is a University of Florida IFAS release bred at the Gulf Coast Research and Education Center specifically for Central Florida and Gulf-latitude winter production.

directions: Plant dormant crowns with the crown at soil level in raised, well-drained beds in full sun; Florida127, sold under the brand name Sweet Sensation, was bred at the University of Florida's Gulf Coast Research and Education Center specifically for the mild winters of Central Florida and similar Gulf-latitude climates. It produces larger fruit and higher yield than the earlier Florida Radiance release, along with a longer shelf life and sweeter flavor that has made it popular with both commercial growers and home gardeners in the region. Like other short-day strawberries in zone 9, treat it as a winter annual, planting fresh crowns each fall for harvest through winter into spring. Maintain consistent drip irrigation and raised, well-drained beds to reduce disease pressure in humid Gulf Coast conditions.
sources: University of Florida IFAS — Gulf Coast Research and Education Center

common_name: Florida Radiance Strawberry (UF/IFAS Gulf-Latitude Short-Day Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant dormant crowns in October–November in zone 9 for a winter-into-spring crop; Florida Radiance is a University of Florida IFAS release that became a dominant short-day strawberry across Florida and Gulf-latitude winter production regions worldwide.

directions: Plant dormant crowns with the crown at soil level in raised, well-drained beds in full sun; Florida Radiance is a University of Florida IFAS-bred short-day strawberry that became one of the most widely planted cultivars in Florida and similar Gulf-latitude winter production regions, prized for its combination of early, high yield and good flavor in warm winter climates unsuited to many Northern-bred strawberry varieties. The bright red, well-formed berries perform reliably through a Gulf South winter growing season. As with other short-day strawberries in zone 9, plant fresh crowns each fall and treat as a winter annual, harvesting from winter into spring before the plants decline in summer heat. Maintain consistent drip irrigation and raised, well-drained beds to reduce disease pressure common in humid Gulf Coast conditions.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Strawberry Variety Trials

common_name: Sweetie Pie Blackberry (Rosette Disease-Resistant Thornless Trailing Type)

planting.note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in late winter through early spring; Sweetie Pie is a USDA-ARS release from the Southern Horticultural Laboratory in Poplarville, Mississippi, bred specifically for resistance to rosette disease (double blossom), the major limiting disease for blackberries across the humid South.

directions: Plant dormant canes 1-2 inches deep in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil, providing a trellis for the trailing canes to climb; Sweetie Pie is a thornless trailing blackberry developed at the USDA-ARS Southern Horticultural Laboratory in Poplarville, Mississippi, bred specifically for resistance to rosette disease (double blossom), a fungal disease that deforms flowers and ruins fruit set and is one of the most serious blackberry problems across the hot, humid South. It produces sweet, well-flavored berries on canes that need training to a trellis since the trailing habit does not stand upright on its own. Because rosette disease spreads through infected plant tissue and is difficult to control with fungicides alone once established, Sweetie Pie's genetic resistance is a real practical advantage for Gulf South growers who have struggled with the disease in other varieties. Prune out fruited floricanes after harvest and train new primocanes onto the trellis for next year's crop.
sources: USDA-ARS Southern Horticultural Laboratory — Poplarville, Mississippi
